findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Month 2 Budget Management Report Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs are forecasted to overspend by £0.302m with household numbers rising above budget assumptions by year-end
findings.detail: At Month 2 there are 260 households in temporary accommodation against a budgeted assumption of 282. However, the forecast assumes growth to 275 households by year end, compared to a budget assumption of 250, resulting in an unfavourable variance of £0.302m.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a demand-led budget that signals housing stress and rising homelessness. Growth above plan indicates demographic or economic pressures that could continue into future years. It is also volatile and difficult to control.
findings.figures: Current households: 260; budgeted: 282; forecast year-end: 275; budgeted year-end: 250; overspend: £0.302m
findings.quote: At month 2 there are 260 households in temporary accommodation, compared to a budgeted assumption of 282 households. However, the forecast assumes growth to 275 households by year end, compared to a budget assumption of 250 households resulting in an unfavourable variance.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Month 2 Budget Management Report Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: Overdue corporate debt stands at £11.432m (£5.981m over 12 months old) with a significant contractor debt and increasing bad debt provision requirement
findings.detail: Sundry debt arrears have reached £11.432m at 31 May 2026, with £5.981m over 12 months old. The most material issue is £1.197m of unpaid invoices from a significant Place directorate contractor; the council notes discussions are ongoing but payment is not yet confirmed. Additionally, £0.658m is owed by NHS for contributions to care. Bad debt provision is forecast to increase from £5.753m to £6.471m, requiring a £0.692m contribution from revenue budgets.
findings.matters: Large aged arrears (over 12 months) indicate collection difficulty and credit risk. The single large contractor debt is a specific vulnerability; if that payment does not materialise, it will crystallise as a loss. Bad debt provisions consume resources and forecast provisioning suggests confidence in collection is declining.
findings.figures: Total overdue debt: £11.432m; debt over 1 year: £5.981m; contractor debt Place directorate: £1.197m; NHS contributions debt: £0.658m; bad debt provision increase: £0.692m; provision as % of debt: 56.6% (was 58.3% at March)
findings.quote: Overdue debt on the corporate ledger, including deferred payments, at 31 May was £11.432m, with debt over 12 months being £5.981m... The most notable reason for the recent increase in arrears is related to significant contractor in the Place directorate, which has £1.197m of unpaid invoices. Discussions have been ongoing and we anticipate a large amount of this debt being settled imminently.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Month 2 Budget Management Report Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: Capital programme has identified £12.378m of slippage with execution risk increasing
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital programme has £12.378m of identified slippage (of which £3.001m is from RBWM-controlled projects). The largest element is £9.377m from the ICB Health Hub due to planned multiyear phasing. Actual expenditure at Month 2 is only 2.6% of forecast. The previous year saw 37% of the budgeted capital programme delay into 2026/27, and the report notes 'there is also an expected risk that the amount of slippage from 2026/27 to 2027/28 (currently 10% of the RBWM controlled projects) will increase.'
findings.matters: Repeated capital slippage (37% last year, further delays expected this year) indicates delivery and project management challenges. Large slippage affects planned savings, service delivery, and funding alignment. It also affects the council's interest and MRP forecasts (lower borrowing due to lower spend means lower financing costs).
findings.figures: Total slippage: £12.378m; ICB Health Hub slippage: £9.377m; actual expenditure Month 2: 1.126m of 43.438m forecast (2.6%); prior year slippage into 2026/27: 37% of budget
findings.quote: Likely slippage of £12.378m has been identified of which £3.001m is presented through RBWM controlled projects. The slippage is principally because of two factors. The most substantial is the planned multiyear phasing of the ICB Health Hub... there is also an expected risk that the amount of slippage from 2026/27 to 2027/28 (currently 10% of the RBWM controlled projects) will increase as the previous year saw approximately 37% of the budgeted capital programme delay into 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Month 2 Budget Management Report Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block faces a £9.150m overspend with a cumulative deficit projected to reach £17.774m, contingent on government grant write-off
findings.detail: Expenditure on the High Needs education block is forecast at £204.156m against a grant allocation of £195.006m. The cumulative DSG deficit will grow from £8.624m at 31 March 2026 to £17.774m by 31 March 2027. A new High Needs Stability Grant will write off 90% of the deficit (reducing it to £10.012m), but the DfE has confirmed only that it 'will take an appropriate and proportionate approach' to future deficits in 2027/28 and 2028/29 — providing no certainty beyond this year.
findings.matters: This is a structural funding failure: the DSG is frozen in cash terms while SEND demand and costs both rise. The council cannot bridge this gap without government grant. The contingency on the Stability Grant being renewed creates medium-term balance sheet risk.
findings.figures: High Needs Block: £9.150m overspend; cumulative DSG deficit: £8.624m rising to £17.774m; after grant write-off: £10.012m; number of young people with EHCPs: 1,403 (up 86 from 1,317 one year prior)
findings.quote: The 2026/27 pressure on the high needs block is being driven by a mismatch between the grant funding being provided to support services for children with special educational needs and/or disabilities and the cost of support. The grant funding was frozen on a cash basis between 2025/26 and 2026/27 despite increasing numbers of young people becoming eligible for support and inflationary pressures.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Month 2 Budget Management Report Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: The council remains dependent on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to fund a significant proportion of its budget, and this is described as unsustainable
findings.detail: The report states explicitly that the council 'remains reliant on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to fund a significant proportion of its budget' and that 'Exceptional financial support is not a sustainable solution to the council's financial challenges.' This indicates ongoing structural budget problems that cannot be resolved within normal spending limits.
findings.matters: A council dependent on government bailout funding faces structural credit risk. The reliance suggests either that underlying demand exceeds resources or that service transformation is not progressing. This will need to resolve for the council to be self-sustaining.
findings.figures: EFS forms a significant but unquantified portion of the budget; the report notes the council 'continues to operate within a challenging financial environment'
findings.quote: The Council continues to operate within a challenging financial environment and remains reliant on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to fund a significant proportion of its budget. Exceptional financial support is not a sustainable solution to the council's financial challenges.

findings.headline: Youth Offending Team relocation tender costs exceed estimate by £0.174m.
findings.detail: The Cranstoun Relocation project, which involves remodelling the Desborough Suite to relocate the Youth Offending Team from Reform Road to Maidenhead Town Hall, is forecasting an overspend of £0.174m because tender evaluation returned bids significantly higher than initially predicted.
findings.matters: Signals weaknesses in project cost estimation during the planning phase. Lenders assess whether the council has reliable project costing and scoping processes, particularly for capital delivery.
findings.figures: £0.174m overspend forecast on relocation remodelling works.
findings.quote: The overspend is projected because the tender evaluation returned bids which were higher than initially predicted.

findings.headline: Stafferton Way Car Park budget increased by £0.200m after survey reveals higher vandalism and additional health & safety works.
findings.detail: Post-budget surveys of Stafferton Way Car Park identified higher levels of vandalism damage than initially assessed and uncovered additional health and safety requirements including replacement of the fire alarm and CCTV systems. This triggered a £0.200m uplift to the project budget.
findings.matters: Illustrates how cost estimating can fall short of actual conditions, requiring significant mid-project increases. The pattern of post-budget cost discovery is relevant to assessing the council's capital project management and delivery capability.
findings.figures: £0.200m uplift required.
findings.quote: A £0.200m uplift to the Stafferton Way Car Park budget has been requested because surveys have determined the level of vandalism to be higher than initially assessed and to encompass an increased scope of works including other health and safety requirements such as a replacement fire alarm and CCTV systems.

findings.headline: School capital allocation cannot be finalized until DfE grant confirmation; £0.363m remains unallocated in April.
findings.detail: The council could not finalize its School Condition Programme budget for 2026/27 until the Department for Education confirmed the grant allocation in April 2026. This left £0.363m of the received grant unallocated four months into the financial year while detailed spending proposals are still being developed.
findings.matters: Demonstrates significant dependency on central government funding timing and creates mid-year budget uncertainty. Cash flow and capital deployment planning cannot be finalized until external grant decisions are made.
findings.figures: £0.363m unallocated; grant confirmation received April 2026.
findings.quote: Budgets were not able to be finalised for 2026/27 until the DfE confirmed the 2026/27 School Condition Allocation which was received April 2026, proposals for the appropriate use of the unallocated sum are being developed.

findings.headline: SEND reform policy pause has deferred £2.338m of High Needs Provision capital investment.
findings.detail: The council was unable to develop capital investment proposals for high needs education provision until the Department for Education released its SEND reforms. Now that these reforms are published, the council plans to bring proposals to Cabinet and public consultation, but this has delayed spending of the full grant allocation to later in 2026.
findings.matters: Shows how external policy decisions create significant delays in council capital planning, affecting when grant funding is actually deployed and impacting cash flow and loan drawdown timing.
findings.figures: £2.338m unallocated from received grant; public consultation planned for later in 2026.
findings.quote: There is £2.338m of the received High Needs Provision Grant currently unallocated because the development of projects was paused as the LA waited for the DfE's SEND reforms. Now that these have been released, the LA will develop proposals for capital investment, to bring to Cabinet and then public consultation, later in 2026.

findings.headline: Housing Service Temporary Accommodation action delayed; progress contingent on recruiting additional staff
findings.detail: The Temporary Accommodation Strategy implementation deadline has slipped from 31 December 2026 to March 2027. The progress update explicitly states that advancement is dependent on recruiting and integrating extra resources into the Housing Service, suggesting current capacity constraints in a potentially high-cost area.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is typically a cost-significant and growing budget pressure for councils. Resource constraints in delivering the strategy suggest the council may struggle to control TA costs and homelessness demand within current staffing levels.
findings.figures: Deadline revised from 31/12/2026 to 31/03/2027
findings.quote: Work on the strategies in officers work programmes but due to capacity issues, progress is dependent on recruiting and integrating extra resources into the Housing Service. This is underway.

findings.headline: Business Continuity Plans only 52% complete; multiple critical service areas still lack current plans
findings.detail: A Priority 1 audit action originally due September 2023 has been extended to July 2026 and remains incomplete. Children services, Communications, Neighbourhood services, and Property have no current plans, and a third of completed plans are out of date. This represents a significant governance gap in operational resilience.
findings.matters: Incomplete business continuity planning exposes the council to operational and service delivery risk. Lenders assessing financial resilience and continuity need confidence in the council's ability to maintain critical functions during disruption.
findings.figures: 52% completion rate; four service areas without current plans
findings.quote: Overall, the percentage of completed Business continuity (BC) plans has slipped slightly from previous reports to 52%. Work continues to be done with various Assistant directors to have their BC plans ready for the start of July. The current areas without a plan that can be shared are Children services, Communications, Neighbourhood services, Property.

findings.headline: Highways inspection and maintenance are under-resourced; we do not have a full complement of staff.
findings.detail: Highways risk rose from 6 to 9 in Q4 and remains at 9 in Q1, above target of 4. The register explicitly states 'We do not have a full complement of staff which is causing issues with the inspection, maintenance and repair of the highway.' An agency inspector commenced mid-June to support, and recruitment for an inspections administrator is progressing, but the gap remains.
findings.matters: Under-resourced highways inspection defers maintenance, increases costs of emergency repairs, and creates liability risk. A staffing gap that requires agency cover is expensive and unstable.
findings.figures: Risk rating Q3 6→Q4 9→Q1 9, target 4; agency inspector commencing mid-June
findings.quote: We do not have a full complement of staff which is causing issues with the inspection, maintenance and repair of the highway.

findings.headline: School building safety risk rating unexpectedly worsened from 4 to 8 in Q1 2026/27.
findings.detail: School building hazards risk rose sharply from 4 to 8 in the latest quarter, a significant deterioration. The risk covers compliance with fire, legionella and asbestos obligations. While the register states ongoing fire surveys, asbestos management and legionella testing are in place, the rating change suggests either new issues have emerged or existing mitigations are not keeping pace with requirements.
findings.matters: A sudden rating rise in school building safety is unusual and suggests a material compliance or resourcing issue has emerged that warrants investigation.
findings.figures: Q3 rating 4, Q4 rating 4, Q1 rating 8
findings.quote: Failure to comply with legislation around and provide a service for monitoring and managing school building related risks such as fire, legionella and asbestos.

findings.headline: Adult safeguarding demand has increased significantly and partnerships are struggling to meet statutory timescales.
findings.detail: Adult safeguarding risk rose from 6 to 9 in Q1 2026/27, moving away from the target of 6. The register notes the council has seen an increase in the number of requests for safeguarding adults reviews and partnerships are under increased pressure to deliver these on time to meet statutory requirements. Work is ongoing to review processes and ensure consistency.
findings.matters: Safeguarding pressure indicates either rising vulnerability in the population or inadequate capacity. Either way, it signals potential service delivery and compliance risk.
findings.figures: Risk rating increased Q3 6→Q4 6→Q1 9, above target of 6
findings.quote: We have seen an increase in the number of requests for safeguarding adults reviews. As a result of these resource demands, partnerships are under increased pressure to get these delivered on time.

findings.headline: Social work and care workforce has 11 vacant posts and recruitment is difficult due to pay scales being uncompetitive.
findings.detail: Workforce stability risk is rated 12/12, well above target of 3. The council faces difficulty recruiting and retaining staff because pay scales are comparatively lower than other local authorities. Adult social care has 11 vacant posts remaining despite salary reviews and retention payments. The council has substantially reduced agency staff but the structural pay competitiveness issue remains. A new workforce plan is in development.
findings.matters: Unfilled social care posts lead to either continued agency spend (which is expensive) or reduced service capacity in a high-risk service. Inability to compete on pay suggests this will persist.
findings.figures: 11 social work posts vacant or covered by locums; 11 vacancies remain in ASCH
findings.quote: Recruitment and stability suffers from comparatively lower pay scales than other local authorities both locally and nationally.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs have been under pressure since 2020/21 and remain at highest risk rating.
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation is rated 12/12, the highest possible risk, with target of 6. Costs have been under pressure for over five years. The council approved a major transformation of housing services in November 2025 to tackle homelessness and reduce reliance on costly temporary accommodation. John West House is complete with services starting early June. Partnership with Registered Housing Providers is in progress and the council is exploring use of its property company, but the risk remains at maximum rating.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is one of the fastest-growing council costs nationally. A five-year trend of pressure and a maximum risk rating indicates the transformation may not be delivering fast enough.
findings.figures: Costs under pressure since 2020/21; John West House services commencing early June 2026
findings.quote: The costs of temporary accommodation could increase beyond the council's capacity to fund. Costs have been under pressure since 2020/21.

findings.headline: Social care market costs are high-risk and ICB is making 50% cuts, threatening jointly funded services.
findings.detail: The social care market risk is rated 12/12 (Q1), above target of 6. The council faces demand pressures for placements in both children's and adults services. The Integrated Care Board is having to make 50% cuts, creating risk that currently funded services may stop or be reduced. The council opened Oak House in-house children's home and has a business case for 22 units of supported accommodation at Imperial Road projected to deliver £216k annual savings.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled placement costs and reductions in joint ICB funding are two of the largest financial exposures facing councils. The council's ability to absorb ICB cuts directly affects social care budget stability.
findings.figures: Projected annual savings approx £216k from Imperial Road accommodation (based on 2025 care prices); ICB 50% cuts
findings.quote: With the ICB having to make 50% cuts there is a risk that currently funded things, even wider than the BCF, may be stopped or reduced.

findings.headline: Pension fund valuation has not improved and remains on track for 2040 full funding only.
findings.detail: The 2025 triennial valuation showed no improvement in the funding level, with the final deficit recovery date remaining static at 2040. The risk is rated 12/12, well above the target of 8. The council is working through options for amending strategic asset allocation, but significant uncertainties remain until the agreed date is reached.
findings.matters: Pension deficits represent long-term obligations that reduce the council's financial flexibility. A static position with no improvement trajectory is concerning.
findings.figures: Deficit recovery date remains 2040; triennial valuation 2025 shows no improvement
findings.quote: The triennial valuation for 2025 has not shown an improvement in the Funding level, but that the final deficit recovery date has remained static at 2040. Significant uncertainties will exist until the agreed date is reached.

findings.headline: In 2028 the DSG statutory override ends, creating an unfunded liability for SEND support.
findings.detail: The DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) override has masked a deficit in special educational needs funding. It expires in 2028, at which point, if the government takes no action, the council will face severe financial pressures. The risk is rated 12/12, above target of 8, and the council has submitted a Local SEND Reform Plan to access a High Needs Stability Grant to write off 90% of historic deficits accrued by end of 2025/26, but future funding remains uncertain.
findings.matters: This is a known cliff-edge liability in two years' time. If government funding does not materialise, the council faces a structural deficit it cannot absorb.
findings.figures: DSG override due to end 2028
findings.quote: In 2028 the DSG statutory override is due to end. If no further action is taken by govt regarding the funding of support for children and young people with special educational needs or disabilities, this will lead to severe financial pressures.

findings.headline: Council is dependent on exceptional MHCLG financial support with no permanent solution visible.
findings.detail: The council agreed an exceptional financial support package for 2026/27 and is in ongoing dialogue with MHCLG about further exceptional support. The Financial Sustainability risk remains at 16/16, well above the target of 8, with general fund reserves only recently strengthened to circa £16m. Budget dependency on transformation programme delivery creates double risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's structural budget position has stabilised or is still materially dependent on one-off government grants that may not continue.
findings.figures: General Fund reserves circa £16m
findings.quote: An exceptional financial support package was agreed with MHCLG for 2026/27. Ongoing dialogue with MHCLG covering future exceptional support requirements following authorisation of support for 26/27.

findings.headline: Council implementing 10.6% council tax increase, relying on government removal of referendum principles to enable rise substantially above normal thresholds
findings.detail: The MTFP requires council tax to grow from £110.251m to £121.992m (an increase of £11.741m or 10.6%). This far exceeds the standard 4.99% maximum that would trigger a local referendum. The council can only implement this increase because government has granted it specific exemption from referendum rules for 2027/28 and 2028/29. The paper states the Section 151 Officer and CEO are clear the council must use the full flexibility available to materially improve its position.
findings.matters: The council has exhausted other revenue options; large council tax increases create political and social risk and demonstrate dependency on government goodwill for exceptional flexibility.
findings.figures: Council tax revenue 2026/27 £110.251m; 2027/28 £121.992m; increase £11.741m (10.6%). Standard referendum threshold 4.99%.
findings.quote: Councils are currently only able to increase council tax by a maximum of 4.99% a year without having to hold a local referendum on the proposed increase. The flexibility given to RBWM from government for 2027/28 and 2028/29 means that the council will be able to decide how to set council tax without the need to hold a referendum in either of these years.

findings.headline: Government may require external CIPFA budget reviews and demonstration of all savings avenues explored as conditions for continued Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: Access to EFS is conditional on the council proving to government that it has explored every avenue for savings. Beyond this, government reserves the right to impose external CIPFA budget reviews on the council. This creates new governance oversight and potential constraints on council autonomy in financial decision-making.
findings.matters: Government-imposed conditions and external reviews represent new governance risks and may constrain the council's operational flexibility in responding to business changes.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The government may also require that RBWM and any other council needing support to set budgets to be subject to further external budget reviews by CIPFA.

findings.headline: Medium-term funding gap deteriorates from £70.760m to £111.911m by 2030/31; EFS costs rise from 6% to 14% of budget
findings.detail: The MTFP shows the structural problem is not temporary but worsening. The funding gap grows by £41.151m over four years. The cost of government support escalates from £11.895m to £33.481m annually, consuming an increasing share of the budget that could otherwise fund services. By 2030/31, fourteen cents of every pound of council spending will service the cost of previous EFS.
findings.matters: A worsening trajectory indicates the council's structural problems are deepening, not stabilizing, creating long-term financial sustainability risk.
findings.quote: the overall message of a significant structural funding gap remains.

findings.headline: Structural deficit of £70.760m in 2027/28 cannot be closed through transformation, savings and income increases; Exceptional Financial Support from government is essential
findings.detail: The council faces a funding gap of £70.760m in 2027/28 between expenditure of £209.802m and available funding of £139.042m. The paper explicitly states the scale of this deficit cannot be closed through the council's own efforts. Government Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) is not optional but mandatory to balance the budget.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council cannot achieve financial sustainability through operational improvements or savings; viability depends entirely on continued government support.
findings.figures: Opening budget 2027/28 £209.802m; government grants £16.243m; council tax £121.992m; business rates £0.807m; total funding £139.042m; funding gap £70.760m
findings.quote: the scale of the structural budget deficit cannot be closed entirely through transformation, savings and increased income, which means the council – as part of the budget process – will again need to engage with government to agree further EFS.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial forecast is 'extremely difficult' with 'significant funding challenges remaining'
findings.detail: Despite a positive 2025-26 outturn with savings over-delivery of £0.382m, the report explicitly states: 'Over the medium-term, the financial forecast for the council remains extremely difficult, with significant funding challenges remaining'. This is stated as the bottom line position after acknowledging the year's improvements.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's view of its own medium-term trajectory. The council is signalling that one year of improved management does not resolve fundamental structural issues.
findings.figures: Medium-term outlook characterised as 'extremely difficult'
findings.quote: However, this year's outturn has demonstrated a greater level of grip on the financial position, with an overall position of a slight underspend on both service and non-service budgets and an over-delivery of savings. This improved position has allowed some additional financial headroom to be built against future financial shocks. This demonstrates really good progress against annual, in-year budget management. Over the medium-term, the financial forecast for the council remains extremely difficult, with significant funding challenges remaining.

findings.headline: Housing temporary accommodation remains structurally overspent at £1.005m due to 'sustained high presentation of homelessness cases'
findings.detail: Despite reducing actual numbers from 304 forecast to 263 actual households, the service overspent by £1.005m on temporary accommodation due to 'sustained high presentation of homelessness cases and the resulting numbers of households placed in temporary accommodation throughout the year, but particularly in the first six months of the year'. The report notes 'the national trend for the number of households in temporary accommodation is increasing each month'.
findings.matters: This is a structural cost pressure driven by national demand increases. It indicates an area where the council's costs are being pushed by external factors (national homelessness crisis) that cannot be controlled locally.
findings.figures: £1.005m overspend on temporary accommodation
findings.quote: The principal driver of the variance against budget was an overspend on temporary accommodation which was £1.005m over budget due to sustained high presentation of homelessness cases and the resulting numbers of households placed in temporary accommodation throughout the year, but particularly in the first six months of the year. This was partly offset by other items, the most significant being a reduction on the Bad Debt Provision of £0.343m.

findings.headline: Eleven of 34 maintained schools are in deficit (£2.670m negative) while system-wide schools funding pressures mount
findings.detail: Of 34 schools, 11 are in deficit (£2.670m total) while only 23 are in surplus (£2.755m total). The council requires schools in deficit to submit recovery plans and implements 'spending control panel' restrictions on essential items only for severe cases.
findings.matters: Schools in deficit represent both a management and cash flow issue for the council. Systemic school deficits can force council bailouts and squeeze other services.
findings.figures: 11 schools in deficit (£2.670m); 23 schools in surplus (£2.755m)
findings.quote: Of the 34 schools, 11 ended the financial year in a deficit position, totalling a negative balance of £2.670m, while 23 ended the financial year with a positive balance, totalling £2.755m.

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £39.076m (61% of budget) with no delivery on ICB Health Hub (£24.355m) and only 37% overall delivery
findings.detail: The council's capital programme of £64.147m delivered only £23.670m (37%), with £39.076m slippage requested. The ICB Health Hub alone accounts for £24.355m (37% of total slippage) with 0% delivery. Remaining slippage includes schools capital (£5.053m), highways (£4.291m) and Temporary Accommodation (£1.445m). The report notes 'a focus of budget monitoring in 2026/27 will be to provide more challenge on slippage as it is an area of the forecast that clearly needs strengthening'.
findings.matters: Significant capital slippage suggests project delivery or project management issues. For a council under financial stress, inability to spend approved capital (which often comes from grants or borrowing) is a concern - it may indicate planning failures, execution failures, or inability to match project schedules.
findings.figures: £39.076m slippage; £24.355m ICB Health Hub (0% delivery); 37% overall delivery rate
findings.quote: The capital programme shows total slippage requested of £39.076m, predominantly due to the ICB Health Hub (£24.355m). Excluding this project, the remaining £14.721m mainly relates to schools' capital (£5.053m), highways and footway construction (£4.291m), and the Temporary Accommodation Local Authority Housing Fund (£1.445m).

findings.headline: A homecare provider failure is now 'highly likely', with anticipated cost increases in 2026-27
findings.detail: The report notes: 'The risk of failure of a Homecare provider due to difficulties obtaining visas for overseas staff that was highlighted in the Month 10 forecast did not materialise during the year; however, the provider's position has further deteriorated, and the risk of failure is now highly likely. The Commissioning Team have been taking proactive steps to prepare for this, with a change of providers anticipated to increase costs in 2026/27.'
findings.matters: This is an identified cost pressure for 2026-27 in a service (Adult Social Care) that is already overspending. A lender needs visibility of identified future cost pressures.
findings.figures: Anticipated cost increase in 2026-27 (amount not specified)
findings.quote: The risk of failure of a Homecare provider due to difficulties obtaining visas for overseas staff that was highlighted in the Month 10 forecast did not materialise during the year; however, the provider's position has further deteriorated, and the risk of failure is now highly likely. The Commissioning Team have been taking proactive steps to prepare for this, with a change of providers anticipated to increase costs in 2026/27.

findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has worsened from £4.514m to £8.624m, a £4.110m deterioration in one year
findings.detail: The High Needs Block alone overspent by £4.671m (on a budget of £26.587m), driven by 'significant increases in complex children whose education was outside a schools setting (£0.898m), Top-up funding for special schools (£1.108m), Mainstream settings (£0.899m) and placements costs for non-maintained and independent special schools (£1.851m)'. The council notes 'it is recognised nationally that the High Needs system within the Dedicated Schools Grant is failing to fund demand'.
findings.matters: Although the Government has pledged to fund 90% of accumulated deficits through SEND Reforms, the council is currently carrying the full burden of an overspend that is growing year-on-year and is acknowledged to be a national policy failure, not a local management issue.
findings.figures: Opening DSG deficit £4.514m; Closing DSG deficit £8.624m; High Needs Block overspend £4.671m
findings.quote: It is recognised nationally that the High Needs system within the Dedicated Schools Grant is failing to fund demand. There has been a Statutory Override in place for a number of years, which has allowed Councils to hold a 'negative reserve' to fund overspends within the High Needs block.

findings.headline: Children's Services placement costs are rising uncontrollably: £2.275m overspend driven by 'increasing volumes and costs'
findings.detail: Social Care Placements alone overspent by £1.376m and are described as driven by 'increasing volumes and costs'. An additional £0.316m overspend on staffing was needed 'to maintain caseloads'. These are not one-off costs but reflect growing demand. A further £0.305m shortfall exists on Unaccompanied Asylum-Seeking Children grant.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether children's services placement costs are spiralling out of control, and whether savings targets can be met if this directorate is uncontrolled.
findings.figures: £2.275m total Children's Services overspend; £1.376m Social Care Placements overspend; £0.316m staffing pressure; £0.305m UASC shortfall
findings.quote: The primary causes of the overspend are increasing volumes and costs within the Social Care Placements budget, leading to an overspend of £1.376m, and an associated staffing pressure of £0.316m to maintain caseloads.

findings.headline: The council is dependent on Exceptional Financial Support of £39.162m to fund a material portion of its budget
findings.detail: The council received £39.162m in government Exceptional Financial Support in 2025-26, used to offset budget shortfalls. Despite an in-year underspend, the council remains 'in a difficult financial situation and dependent on Exceptional Financial Support to fund a considerable proportion of its budget'. This support reduces by only £1.251m from the £39.162m total even after this year's surplus.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can operate without ongoing government bailout, or whether EFS is structural and indefinite.
findings.figures: £39.162m EFS; only £1.251m reduction in EFS requirement despite £3.079m underspend
findings.quote: notes that in the light of the underspend position, unallocated funds received in year of £1.251m will be used to reduce the level of exceptional financial support applied, which is £39.162m in total

findings.headline: The council continues to rely on savings overachievement to meet budget, having delivered £6m savings in 2024-25 and forecast £6.4m in 2025-26.
findings.detail: The council describes managing within budget in 2025-26 but is relying on forecast overachievement of savings to do so. The track record shows £6m delivered in 2024-25 and £6.4m forecast for 2025-26. The council is procuring a specialist transformation partner to identify and deliver further savings at pace. This pattern suggests structural budget deficit rather than one-time issues.
findings.matters: Persistent reliance on savings overachievement, even as amounts grow, indicates an underlying structural funding gap that cannot be closed by incremental improvement alone.
findings.figures: £6m savings delivered 2024-25; £6.4m forecast 2025-26
findings.quote: The council's track record of delivering savings has improved significantly over the past few years, with the council of course to over deliver savings in 2025/26 (£6.4m) on top of the delivery of £6m savings in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Internal audit found the council had not demonstrated its shareholder responsibilities in Optalis, the jointly-owned adult social care company.
findings.detail: During 2025-26, internal audit identified concerns about the council's shareholder role in Optalis, a jointly owned company providing adult social care services. While service oversight and commissioning reviews were in place, there was little evidence of the council demonstrating its ownership responsibilities. A Shareholder Panel has been convened in response, with annual report and three-year business plan produced.
findings.matters: Failure of shareholder oversight in a council-owned service delivery company indicates a governance gap and potential value-for-money risk in the largest service area (adult social care).
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: During the 25/26 year, internal audit identified a number of concerns relating to the demonstration of the council's shareholder role in relation to Optalis, a jointly owned company providing adult social care services as a proxy for in-house services. While service oversight and commissioning reviews of performance and value for money were in place, there was little evidence of the council demonstrating its ownership responsibilities.

findings.headline: The fixed asset register required validation due to concerns identified in 2024-25 accounts preparation, with implementation continuing into 2025-26.
findings.detail: Preparation of 2024-25 accounts highlighted concerns over the approach to maintaining the fixed asset register. A plan was developed and implemented during 2025-26 to re-validate the register and put it in a format conducive to accurate accounting, as part of the finance transformation plan.
findings.matters: Fixed asset register errors can misstate both the balance sheet and capital financing arrangements, and indicate broader data quality issues.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Preparation of the 2024/25 accounts highlighted concerns over the approach to maintaining the fixed asset register. A plan was developed and implemented during 2025/26 to re-validate the fixed asset register and put it in a format conducive to accurate accounting going forward.

findings.headline: The council acknowledges that financial records require further work to reach good quality standard.
findings.detail: The council states it recognises that further work is required to ensure financial records are considered good quality. This follows recent strengthening of the finance team and recruitment of a permanent Section 151 officer in 2025-26.
findings.matters: Poor financial record quality undermines the reliability of financial reporting and governance, affecting both internal control and external audit.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The council does, however, recognise that further work is required to ensure our financial records are considered good quality.

findings.headline: External audit identified significant weaknesses in financial and governance arrangements in 2024-25, with some audit work incomplete at the statutory backstop date.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton concluded their work on the 2024-25 Statement of Accounts but could not complete all audit work by the backstop date. The audit report identified significant weaknesses in financial and governance arrangements. The council also notes a high number of overdue audit actions persisting, including in key risk areas.
findings.matters: Incomplete audit work and identified significant weaknesses at a backstop date indicate internal control failures and raise questions about financial statement reliability.
findings.figures: High number of overdue audit actions in key risk areas; significant amount of 2024-25 audit work could not be completed by backstop date
findings.quote: External audit concluded their work on the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts and these were published by the statutory backstop date. A significant amount of audit work was completed but there was also audit work which could not be completed to meet the backstop date. There were also significant weaknesses in financial and governance arrangements identified during the audit work

findings.headline: The council wrote to government in early 2024 about the risk of issuing a statutory Section 114 notice due to structural funding shortfall.
findings.detail: In early 2024, the Leader and Cabinet Member for Finance wrote jointly to the Chancellor and Secretary of State setting out the risk of a Section 114 notice. The council's baseline funding is around £30 million lower due to historical council tax cuts over 2010-2018, and a further £30 million loss is projected from the fair funding review. The council is in proactive discussions with MHCLG for Exceptional Financial Support, though the 7.49% council tax increase permitted in 2026-27 is described as insufficient to close the shortfall.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal declaration that a council cannot balance its budget and is a critical governance and credit event for lenders.
findings.figures: £30 million baseline funding shortfall from historical decisions; further £30 million loss from fair funding review; 7.49% council tax increase in 2026-27 deemed insufficient
findings.quote: In early 2024, the Leader of the Council and Cabinet Member for Finance wrote jointly to the Chancellor and Secretary of State setting out the risk of the council having to issue a statutory Section 114 notice.

findings.headline: Capital programme forecast to spike to £52m in 2026/27, doubling the prior year
findings.detail: Capital expenditure is forecast to jump from £23.67m in 2025/26 to £52.215m in 2026/27. Combined with £48.754m in capitalisation directive spending that same year, this large programme will drive substantial new borrowing and accelerate the rise in financing costs already forecast for 2026/27.
findings.matters: A sharp increase in planned capital spending will require significant additional borrowing at a time when the council already faces budget pressure and depends on exceptional financial support.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure 2025/26 £23.67m; 2026/27 forecast £52.215m; capitalisation directive 2026/27 £48.754m
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure: 2025/26 Actual £23.670m, 2026/27 Forecast £52.215m; Capitalisation Directive: 2026/27 Forecast £48.754m

findings.headline: Long-term borrowing forecast to rise to £365m by 2027/28 due to Fair Funding Review impact
findings.detail: The CFR is forecast to increase from £317.79m (2025/26) to £364.97m (2027/28). This reflects the government's Fair Funding Review 2.0 making the council more dependent on borrowing. The liability benchmark (estimated long-term borrowing need) is forecast to reach £312.724m by 2027/28, confirming the council will remain a substantial long-term borrower.
findings.matters: Increasing structural borrowing need commits the council to sustained debt market access and raises refinancing risk if market conditions deteriorate or borrowing appetite declines.
findings.figures: CFR 2025/26 £317.79m; CFR forecast 2027/28 £364.97m; liability benchmark 2027/28 £312.724m
findings.quote: Fair Funding Review 2.0 has made the council more dependent on borrowing and without a significant change in funding the council will see the underlying need to borrow increase.

findings.headline: Financing costs forecast to consume 23% of available revenue by 2027/28
findings.detail: The share of net revenue spent on debt interest and minimum revenue provision is forecast to rise from 14.52% (2025/26 actual) to 23.21% (2027/28). In cash terms this means financing costs rising from £19.619m to £32.272m. This trajectory leaves the council with severely constrained resources for service delivery.
findings.matters: Rapidly rising financing costs crowd out money available for services and reduce the council's capacity to absorb shocks or manage emerging pressures.
findings.figures: 2025/26 actual: £19.619m (14.52% of revenue); 2027/28 forecast: £32.272m (23.21% of revenue)
findings.quote: Proportion of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream: 2025/26 actual 14.52%, 2026/27 forecast 18.80%, 2027/28 forecast 23.21%

findings.headline: Council remains dependent on exceptional financial support to balance the budget
findings.detail: Windsor and Maidenhead uses a capitalisation directive to set a balanced budget. The CFR increased by £32.39m to £317.79m in 2025/26, driven by £39.162m of EFS-treated spending. The forecast assumes EFS will be needed for at least five years of the medium-term financial plan, with no indicated exit route.
findings.matters: Continued reliance on exceptional financial support signals structural budget imbalance and limits the council's financial flexibility and debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: CFR £317.79m (2025/26); EFS capitalisation directive £39.162m; forecast CFR £364.97m (2027/28)
findings.quote: the council's need for exceptional financial support (EFS) to set a balanced budget... Fair Funding Review 2.0 has made the council more dependent on borrowing and without a significant change in funding the council will see the underlying need to borrow increase.

findings.headline: Two breaches of prudential treasury limits during 2025/26
findings.detail: The council breached the limit on investments held beyond the year end (£15.162m actual vs £15.0m limit) and the limit on cash available within 3 months (£23.047m actual vs £24.686m target). Both breaches resulted from an unbudgeted investment made in the last quarter. The council has agreed to review prudential indicators at bi-monthly treasury board meetings.
findings.matters: Breaches of treasury controls indicate governance gaps and reveal tight liquidity in a council already dependent on exceptional financial support.
findings.figures: Investment beyond year-end £15.162m vs £15.0m limit; cash within 3 months £23.047m vs £24.686m target
findings.quote: During the year there were two minor breaches of our prudential limits, both linked to the same issue. The limit for the value of investments held over the year end was breached because an investment was made in the last quarter of the year which was greater than the amount previously forecast. The total cash available for the next 3 months was also breached, caused by the same additional investment as this reduced the amount of cash available.

findings.paper_title: ITEM 7a Appendix A Berkshire Pension Fund Audit Findings Report 2024-25 25-02-2026
findings.headline: Audit completion delayed due to investment manager confirmation delays.
findings.detail: Auditors encountered significant delays obtaining confirmations from fund managers, impacting delivery of audit work. Audit planned completion was December 2025 but work extended into February 2026, partly due to delayed responses from investment managers.
findings.matters: External dependency on investment managers' responsiveness creates risk of future audit delays and compliance failures; indicates potential governance issues with investment manager oversight.
findings.figures: Planned completion December 2025; actual completion February 2026; report issued 25 February 2026
findings.quote: The audit team have encountered delays in obtaining confirmations from the fund managers and due to the review of the longevity swap valuation by our internal experts.

findings.paper_title: ITEM 7a Appendix A Berkshire Pension Fund Audit Findings Report 2024-25 25-02-2026
findings.headline: Repeated control failure: journal transaction dates outside financial year not corrected from prior year.
findings.detail: Auditors identified the same control weakness in 2023-24 and 2024-25: journals posted with created dates outside the financial year due to transposition errors. Despite management's commitment to address this via user training and approval controls, the issue persists in 2024-25, requiring additional audit work.
findings.matters: Unresolved control weaknesses over transaction dating indicate that management's commitment to remediation cannot be relied upon and raise questions about the robustness of internal control over transaction recording.
findings.figures: Issue identified in 2023-24 audit; repeated in 2024-25; affects multiple transactions
findings.quote: This has remained an issue for 24/25. The audit team have identified multiple instances of transactions being posted with created dates outside the 24/25 financial year. This has resulted in increased work for the audit team in gaining assurance over the validity of these transactions.

findings.paper_title: ITEM 7a Appendix A Berkshire Pension Fund Audit Findings Report 2024-25 25-02-2026
findings.headline: Accounts production delayed past statutory deadline with core disclosures incomplete in draft submission.
findings.detail: The fund did not produce complete draft accounts by the statutory 30 June 2025 deadline; accounts published on 30 June lacked required longevity swap and other key disclosures, which were only updated after audit fieldwork began in October 2025. This pattern creates compliance risk and impacts audit timeline.
findings.matters: Persistent failure to meet statutory deadlines impairs transparency and triggers backstop legislation penalties; it also signals control and resource issues in the finance function.
findings.figures: Statutory audit deadline 28 February 2026; accounts initially incomplete on 30 June 2025; core disclosures added October 2025
findings.quote: The accounts published on the 30th of June were not complete as the Pension Fund did not have the required information for some disclosures including the longevity swap valuation. These were updated after the start of our audit fieldwork start date in early October.

findings.paper_title: ITEM 7a Appendix A Berkshire Pension Fund Audit Findings Report 2024-25 25-02-2026
findings.headline: Longevity insurance contract valued outside auditor's reasonable valuation range.
findings.detail: The contract is valued at £139.2m in the financial statements, but the auditors' internal expert determined a reasonable range of £99.4m to £136.2m, meaning the recorded value overstates liabilities by £3m. This is a significant estimation uncertainty on a major liability.
findings.matters: Pension fund liabilities are a critical metric for assessing the fund's sustainability and the council's long-term financial obligations; misstated liabilities affect funding requirements and employer contribution rates.
findings.figures: Recorded value £139.2m; auditor expert range £99.4m to £136.2m; overstatement £3m
findings.quote: Our expert has determined a reasonable valuation range. The value reported in the Financial statements of (£139.2m) sits outside this range and we are therefore reporting the difference (£3m) as a nonmaterial misstatement, overstating liabilities in the draft financial statements.

findings.paper_title: ITEM 7a Appendix A Berkshire Pension Fund Audit Findings Report 2024-25 25-02-2026
findings.headline: £2.3m of unadjusted investment valuation differences identified but not corrected in the accounts.
findings.detail: Auditors identified three separate investment valuation issues totalling £2.3m: £3m overstatement in longevity insurance contract, £8.9m overstatement in Level 3 investments, and £5.32m overstatement in Level 2 investments. Management has elected not to adjust these, treating them as immaterial despite exceeding the £3m reporting threshold.
findings.matters: Unadjusted valuation errors totalling £17.2m across the fund's £3.1bn asset base signal control weaknesses in investment valuation processes and raise questions about management's ability to identify and correct material errors.
findings.figures: £2.3m total unadjusted differences; materiality threshold £3m; total net assets £3.13bn
findings.quote: We have identified £2.3m of unadjusted differences in the valuation of the Fund's investments and liabilities disclosed in the financial statements at 31 March 2025 and the valuation statements received from the third-party investment managers.

findings.paper_title: ITEM 7a Appendix A Berkshire Pension Fund Audit Findings Report 2024-25 25-02-2026
findings.headline: Audit opinion will be modified due to unresolved opening balances from prior year backstop disclaimer.
findings.detail: The prior year audit resulted in a disclaimed opinion due to backstop legislation. The auditors have been unable to obtain sufficient assurance on opening balances for the comparator year, requiring a modified opinion on the 2024-25 statements. This limits the assurance users can rely on when assessing the fund's financial position.
findings.matters: A modified audit opinion reduces stakeholder confidence in the financial statements and may constrain the council's access to credit markets or trigger additional scrutiny from rating agencies.
findings.figures: Audit opinion issued 25 February 2026, after the 28 February 2026 backstop deadline
findings.quote: we have been unable to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion in advance of the backstop date of 28 February 2026. The limitations imposed by not having assurance on opening balances mean that we will we need to modify our opinion on the financial statements.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support is a systemic problem affecting at least 30 councils in 2025/26 and more in 2026/27; local government funding system is 'effectively broken'
findings.detail: The CFO states that 30 councils required EFS to set their 2025/26 budgets and the figure is expected to be higher for 2026/27. This is not an isolated problem affecting only poorly-managed authorities. The CFO's assessment is explicit: 'This shows that the local government funding system is effectively broken, and councils are facing systemic challenges.' The implication is that EFS is not a sanction or rescue mechanism but an endemic feature of local government finance under current policy.
findings.matters: A lender looking at RBWM's reliance on EFS might assume this is a management issue unique to the authority. In fact, it is a system-wide feature. This affects the riskiness calculus: RBWM is not uniquely incompetent, but it is caught in a broken funding regime shared by dozens of other councils. Government appetite to continue approving EFS at scale is unclear if this continues to escalate.
findings.figures: 30 councils on EFS in 2025/26; number expected to rise in 2026/27. RBWM borrowing requirement through EFS: £48.754m (2026/27), cumulative of £290.748m over 2026/27-2030/31 per MTFP table.
findings.quote: In total, 30 councils required EFS support to set their 2025/26 budgets and we are told this figure will be higher for 2026/27. This shows that the local government funding system is effectively broken, and councils are facing systemic challenges.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review leaves Windsor and Maidenhead with second-lowest Fair Funding Assessment nationally; business rates baseline cut from £16.3m to £0.8m
findings.detail: The government's Fair Funding Review, implemented for 2026/27 onwards, has redistributed funding away from less-deprived authorities. RBWM is one of the most severely affected. By 2028/29, RBWM will have the second-lowest Fair Funding Assessment (business rates baseline + revenue support grant) of any local authority nationally—including district councils that provide a much narrower range of services. Business rates baseline will fall from £16.294m (2025/26) to £0.793m (2026/27), a cut of 95%, partially mitigated by grant but with that grant also declining over time.
findings.matters: This is a structural, unfixable funding disadvantage baked into the settlement for the medium term. It is not due to RBWM's choices or performance but to the national allocation formula. It drives the entire deficit and makes self-sufficiency impossible without extreme council tax increases. A lender must understand this is a permanent feature, not a cycle.
findings.figures: Business rates: £16.294m retained (2025/26) → £0.793m (2026/27) → 'negligible or disappearing' (2028/29). Revenue Support Grant: £13.714m (2025/26) → £20.241m (2026/27—temporary boost) → £1.673m (2028/29 onwards). Total funding gap vs current: £30m worse off by 2028/29.
findings.quote: By 2028/29, RBWM is expected to have the second lowest FFA of any local authority nationally - including district councils that provide a much narrower range of services. This means that by April 2028 to set a balanced budget the council will be required to use council tax to fund 95% of the cost of local services, compared to an average of 56% nationally.

findings.headline: Prior year overspend of £19.994m on social care and housing; all expenditure over £500 now requires CFO panel approval
findings.detail: In 2024/25, the council overspent by £19.994m on demand-led services (children's and adult social care, temporary accommodation). This overspend was absorbed through contingency and other mechanisms, but it demonstrates the volatility of these budgets. To prevent recurrence, all expenditure items over £500 now require approval by a spending control panel chaired by the S151 Officer. This is an unusually tight control and signals that prior budget management was insufficient. The council is now 'on track' for 2025/26 within envelope (including contingency), but this required extraordinary spending controls.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether budget controls are adequate. The need for panel approval on items over £500 indicates prior controls failed. It also limits the council's operational flexibility—decisions on small items must go to the CFO. This is appropriate risk management but reflects prior failure.
findings.figures: 2024/25 overspend: £19.994m. Contingency held in 2026/27 budget: £5m (with separate assessment of best/middle/worst case scenarios for social care, children's placements, temporary accommodation). Demand-led budget growth: £14.201m (2026/27).
findings.quote: This is a significant improvement on the previous financial year which saw an overspend of £19.994 million and reflects both more robust budget setting and ongoing financial management. All items of expenditure over £500 are still required to be approved by a spending control panel which I chair

findings.headline: Governance and audit assurance at low level; prior year accounts disclaimed, internal audit giving limited assurance, and high corporate risks outstanding
findings.detail: The 2024/25 draft accounts received a disclaimed opinion (auditors could not form a view on opening balances from prior year). The external audit therefore cannot provide full assurance on current year accounts. The Internal Auditor's annual opinion for 2024/25 is 'limited assurance', reflecting the number of limited assurance audits, outstanding recommendations, and high corporate risks remaining. Prior year had 9 external audit VfM recommendations; this year reduced to 6, showing slow improvement. Governance improvement actions carry forward from prior year.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on audited accounts for verifying the council's true financial position. The disclaimed opinion means opening balances are unverified. Limited internal audit assurance indicates unresolved control weaknesses. This creates risk that the council's stated position masks unknown liabilities or misstatements.
findings.figures: General fund balance forecast £15m at 31 March 2026 (CFO states this is minimum acceptable). Earmarked reserves £7.598m. Schools reserves in net deficit position.
findings.quote: Due to the disclaimed opinion on previous year's accounts the audit opinion will not be able to offer full assurance, as the opening balances were not audited previously and the full set of audit work could not be completed by the backstop date.

findings.headline: Debt servicing costs escalating from 14% of budget to 25% by 2030/31; now requires £31m annually on borrowing costs
findings.detail: The cost of servicing debt accumulated through capitalisation directions is forecast at £10.180m in 2026/27 and growing to £31.877m (11.9% of budget) by 2030/31. As a proportion of total budget, debt servicing will rise from 14% to 25% over this period. All existing debt is at fixed interest rates, reducing rate risk on current portfolio, but new borrowing does carry rate exposure managed by treasury advisors.
findings.matters: Escalating debt servicing leaves increasingly little budget for service delivery. A lender assessing the sustainability of council borrowing must see whether the council has a credible plan to stabilise or reduce this. The answer appears to be: only if council tax reaches national average. Otherwise, debt servicing becomes the largest single budget item within five years.
findings.figures: Debt servicing: £10.180m (2026/27) rising to £31.877m (2030/31). As % of budget: 14% (2026/27) rising to 25% (2030/31). Non-debt-service budget: £175.972m (2026/27) declining as proportion of total.
findings.quote: The forecast is for debt servicing to increase from 14% of the budget in 2026/27 to 25% in 2030/31.

findings.headline: DSG deficit could reach £20m by March 2028 and council may not have reserves to cover it, potentially triggering Section 114 notice
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) reserve shows a deficit forecast of £9.870m at 31 March 2026, growing at an accelerating rate. Government will fund 90% of the deficit accrued up to that date in 2026/27, but the statutory override protecting councils from accounting for this deficit ends April 2028. The CFO states the remaining deficit could reach £20m by that date. If the council is required to make good this full amount from its other reserves, it cannot do so. This would force the council to seek additional EFS; if government refuses, the S151 Officer would have 'no choice but to issue a S114 notice' (a declaration of effective insolvency).
findings.matters: This is a sword of Damocles over the authority's financial position. The DSG deficit is driven by SEND costs over which the council has limited control. The government's own SEND white paper has been delayed to 2026. A lender cannot predict whether the authority will face a statutory insolvency declaration in two years.
findings.figures: DSG deficit: £9.870m forecast 31 March 2026. Potential deficit by March 2028: 'up to £20million'. High needs block funding frozen at 2025/26 levels for two years, so annual deficit continues to grow.
findings.quote: The scale of the deficit that will remain in March 2028 could be up to £20million and should the council be required to make good this deficit in full, from its other reserves, it will be unable to do so. This would therefore require the council to seek additional EFS and if this were not forthcoming, I would have no choice but to issue a S114 notice.

findings.headline: Council tax now at 96% of funding by 2029/30; CFO demands catch-up to national average by April 2028 or financial sustainability is 'severely weakened'
findings.detail: The council cut council tax for six successive years, leaving it £30-35m annually below where it otherwise would be. Fair Funding Review has removed a further £30m over three years. By 2029/30, council tax will fund 96% of the budget compared to a national average of 56%. The S151 Officer states in the strongest terms that council tax must reach national average by April 2028; without this, reliance on exceptional financial support becomes unsustainable. If this deadline is missed, a 32.59% increase (£540 on Band D) may be needed in 2028/29 alone to catch up.
findings.matters: Council tax dependency at 96% leaves the authority with no fiscal buffer and places extreme burden on residential taxpayers. A lender must assess whether the political appetite exists to deliver the required increases, and what happens to service delivery and the authority's standing if it does not. The CFO's unusually forceful language ('strongest possible terms', financial sustainability 'severely weakened') signals high risk.
findings.figures: Council tax £1,263.90 (base) + £240.51 (social care precept) = £1,504.41 Band D for 2026/27 (7.49% increase). National average comparator authorities range from £1,539 to £1,763 Band D. By 2028/29, forecast increases of £151.06 (10%) then catch-up needed of £540+ (32.59%) to reach average.
findings.quote: I recommend in the strongest possible terms that the council needs to take the necessary decisions to ensure that the local share of council tax is at the national average level by no later than April 2028. ... Conversely, if this advice is not followed and council tax remains below the national average over an extended period, the financial sustainability of the authority would be severely weakened.

findings.headline: Structural deficit now permanent; council reliant on capitalisation direction to balance budget
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget gap is £48.754m, entirely covered by an exceptional financial support capitalisation direction approved by the Secretary of State. The medium-term plan shows this gap growing to £66.7m (2027/28), £88.5m (2028/29), and £96m (2029/30). The council cannot close these gaps through savings—already at statutory minimum service levels and declared 'lean' on operating costs.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council has capacity to manage debt. Capitalisation directions are not new money but permission to borrow more, spreading costs over 20 years. This is a compounding cycle with escalating debt servicing, not a path to financial recovery.
findings.figures: Budget gap: £48.754m (2026/27), growing to £103.773m by 2030/31. Debt servicing forecast to rise from £10.180m (2026/27) to £31.877m (2030/31)
findings.quote: To be clear, this is not additional money for the council, merely permission to spread the accounting of yearly expenditure over 20 years and to borrow additional money to pay for this. This is a compounding cycle that means debt servicing costs will continue to increase as a proportion of the budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - Capital and Treasury Strategy
findings.headline: Asset condition surveys identify poor condition of council assets requiring substantial maintenance investment
findings.detail: The council is currently undertaking asset condition surveys to establish an evidence-based maintenance programme. The fact that surveys are needed to 'start to address' poor asset condition suggests a backlog of deferred maintenance.
findings.matters: This indicates a hidden capital liability. Deferred maintenance eventually becomes urgent and expensive, and creates additional borrowing pressure.
findings.figures: Asset condition surveys underway to address poor condition
findings.quote: Carrying out asset condition surveys to establish an evidence-based maintenance programme for inclusion in the medium-term financial plan, which will help start to address the poor condition of many assets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - Capital and Treasury Strategy
findings.headline: Council's debt reduction plan depends entirely on achieving £31.562m asset sales in 2026/27, dropping to £19.783m in 2027/28
findings.detail: The capital financing plan assumes all future capital receipts from asset sales will be applied to reduce borrowing. Table F5 shows forecast asset sales declining after 2026/27. If these sales do not proceed as planned, the council has no fallback mechanism to manage its debt trajectory.
findings.matters: Over-reliance on asset sales as the primary means to reduce debt creates execution risk. If the property market softens or sales are delayed, the council's debt will continue to grow unchecked.
findings.quote: The working assumption is that all future capital receipts are applied to reduce the borrowing requirements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - Capital and Treasury Strategy
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing 33% in three years, from £325.526m to £431.774m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The cumulative debt requirement continues to accelerate. Without further increases in baseline funding from government, the council will need to borrow an additional £106m over three years. This trajectory suggests the council cannot self-fund from retained revenue.
findings.matters: Unsustainable debt growth indicates the council's financial position is worsening, not stabilizing. Lenders need evidence of a path back to sustainability, not accelerating deficits.
findings.quote: Capital Financing Requirement: 2026/27 budget £325.526m, 2027/28 estimate £367.286m, 2028/29 estimate £431.774m

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - Capital and Treasury Strategy
findings.headline: Financing costs are forecast to reach 25% of net revenue stream by 2028/29, up from 16% in 2026/27
findings.detail: Interest payable on loans and Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) will consume an escalating share of the council's revenue budget as debt grows. This leaves progressively less for actual service spending and represents an unsustainable trajectory if continued.
findings.matters: Rapidly rising financing costs are crowding out service expenditure and indicate the structural deficit is worsening, not improving. This limits the council's ability to respond to service demands or invest in improvements.
findings.quote: Financing costs (£m): 2026/27 budget 25.772, 2027/28 budget 32.373, 2028/29 budget 40.095. Proportion of net revenue stream: 2026/27 15.97%, 2027/28 19.73%, 2028/29 25.00%

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - Capital and Treasury Strategy
findings.headline: Council's budget setting depends entirely on receiving a government capitalisation directive that treats revenue as capital spending
findings.detail: The council has received exceptional financial support from 2024/25 onwards as a capitalisation directive, which allows revenue costs to be capitalised. The strategy explicitly assumes this will continue for 2026/27 and beyond, with confirmation expected in late February 2026. Without this directive, the council cannot balance its budget.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has structural balance or is dependent on year-to-year government support. This reveals structural deficit that cannot be closed without exceptional help.
findings.figures: £48.754m exceptional financial support budgeted for 2026/27
findings.quote: This strategy assumes that a capitalisation directive will be received for 2026/27 and future years to allow a balanced budget to be set. Confirmation of the 2026/27 capitalisation directive is expected in late February 2026.

findings.headline: Audit certificate cannot be issued; completion delayed pending resolution of an open objection
findings.detail: Grant Thornton cannot formally conclude the audit or issue an audit certificate until receiving NAO confirmation and completing consideration of an open objection raised under section 27 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2024.
findings.matters: An unresolved objection raises questions about what external parties have found; audit certification cannot complete while outstanding.
findings.figures: Section 27, Local Audit and Accountability Act 2024
findings.quote: cannot formally conclude the audit and issue an audit certificate until we have completed our consideration of an open objection brought to our attention under section 27 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2024

findings.headline: The audit itself was defective in its ability to detect irregularities and fraud
findings.detail: Grant Thornton explicitly states the audit was defective in detecting fraud because they could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence due to the same matters that led to the disclaimer of opinion.
findings.matters: An audit unable to detect fraud means there is unquantified fraud risk within the council; combined with control weaknesses this is a material concern for lenders.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document
findings.quote: The audit was defective in its ability to detect irregularities, including fraud, on the basis that we were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

findings.headline: Longstanding procurement and contract management weaknesses with outstanding audit recommendations from 2022-23
findings.detail: Grant Thornton identified a significant weakness in longstanding procurement and contract management issues, including outstanding internal audit recommendations from 2022-23 and insufficient evidence that contract procedure rules were being applied consistently. This weakness remained at 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: Weak procurement controls increase fraud and waste risk; recommendations outstanding for multiple years show governance failure and poor management discipline.
findings.figures: Outstanding recommendations from 2022-23
findings.quote: longstanding weaknesses in procurement and contract management, including outstanding Internal Audit recommendations from 2022/23 and insufficient evidence that contract procedure rules were being applied consistently across the organisation

findings.headline: Governance weaknesses in oversight of major development projects following insourcing of former property company
findings.detail: Grant Thornton identified a significant weakness in the Authority's oversight of major development projects, with need to strengthen governance, scrutiny and monitoring of key financial and delivery risks following insourcing of the former property company. This weakness remained at 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: Property development projects create significant financial exposure; weak oversight following insourcing suggests increased financial and delivery risk.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document
findings.quote: Authority's oversight of major development projects, including the need to strengthen governance, scrutiny and monitoring of key financial and delivery risks following the insourcing of the Authority's former property company

findings.headline: Three consecutive years of backstopped or disclaimed financial statements with unresolved historic accounting errors
findings.detail: Grant Thornton identified a significant weakness relating to continuing risks from three years of backstopped or disclaimed financial statements, historic accounting errors, and inadequate processes for accurate account preparation. This weakness remained unresolved at 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: Three consecutive years of failed audits shows systematic accounting failure; unresolved historic errors mean the council's financial position is unreliable.
findings.figures: Three years of backstopped or disclaimed statements
findings.quote: continuing risks arising from three years of backstopped or disclaimed financial statements, historic accounting errors and the need to improve processes supporting the timely and accurate preparation of accounts

findings.headline: Internal control environment is weak with insufficient internal audit coverage
findings.detail: Grant Thornton identified significant weaknesses: ongoing limitations in the internal control environment, historical lack of internal audit coverage, and slower-than-required implementation of audit recommendations. These weaknesses remained at 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: Weak internal controls and audit increase fraud and financial misstatement risk; slow implementation of recommendations suggests management is not addressing findings.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document
findings.quote: ongoing limitations in the internal control environment, the historical lack of internal audit coverage and slower-than-required implementation of internal audit recommendations

findings.headline: Savings plans are insufficiently developed and underperforming against targets
findings.detail: Grant Thornton identified a significant weakness in insufficiently developed medium-term savings plans, underperformance against savings targets, and need to strengthen the rigour and evidence base for proposals. This weakness remained at 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: Weak savings delivery threatens financial sustainability; underperformance suggests the council cannot meet its budget assumptions.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document
findings.quote: insufficiently developed medium‑term savings plans, underperformance against savings targets, and the need for the Authority to strengthen the rigour, ambition and evidence base supporting savings proposals

findings.headline: The Authority has depleted reserves and cannot demonstrate how to restore them
findings.detail: Grant Thornton identified a significant weakness: the Authority's inability to demonstrate reserve replenishment over the medium term following discovery of historical accounting errors, depleted reserves, and reliance on Exceptional Financial Support. This weakness remained at 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves indicate financial vulnerability; inability to restore them suggests structural budget problems and reliance on government bailouts.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document
findings.quote: inability to demonstrate how it would replenish and maintain adequate reserve levels over the medium term following the discovery of historical accounting errors, depleted reserves and reliance on Exceptional Financial Support

findings.headline: Grant Thornton has issued a disclaimer of opinion on the 2024-25 financial statements
findings.detail: The auditors could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence by the statutory deadline to form an audit opinion. The Authority also failed to present required group accounts statements (Movement in Reserves and Cash Flow Statement), which would have required an adverse opinion if the audit had been completed.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means financial statements cannot be relied upon; lenders cannot assess the council's true financial position.
findings.figures: 27 February 2026 (backstop date)
findings.quote: We do not express an opinion on the accompanying financial statements of the Authority or the group. Because of the significance of the matters described in the basis for disclaimer of opinion section of our report, we have not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide a basis for an audit opinion on these financial statements.

news_drafts.headline: Temporary accommodation costs are forecasted to overspend by £0.302m with household numbers rising above budget assumptions by year-end
news_drafts.lead: Temporary accommodation is a demand-led budget that signals housing stress and rising homelessness. Growth above plan indicates demographic or economic pressures that could continue into future years. It is also volatile and difficult to control.
